name: Kagúru
confidence_why: Last 1886 states that the accent falls almost invariably on the penultimate syllable and Hyman 2013 lists Kagulu among the Bantu languages with penultimate lengthening, but the modern grammar Petzell 2008 reportedly gives examples of pre-antepenultimate stress, which Kraska-Szlenk 2008 finds unconvincing and reads as possibly initial, and that grammar's stress pages could not be consulted directly. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Last 1886.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; it is recomputed over suffixed forms (shifts rightward to stay penultimate). A few lexical exceptions carry non-penultimate accent, which Last marks with an acute (e.g. mehékulu, antepenultimate).
new_statements.exceptions: 'almost invariable' — occasional words with accent elsewhere, marked with an acute in Last's spelling (mehékulu 'a married woman'; demonstratives with final-vowel stress for distal emphasis, p. 44 snippet: '..stress is on the final vowel, so much the more is the distance denoted'). NB the modern grammar (Petzell 2008: 40-41), seen only second-hand via Kraska-Szlenk's 2008 review, apparently hedges: 'there is probably phrasal tone and not lexical tone' and gives examples of 'pre-antepenult' stress, which the reviewer suggests may be initial stress; Hyman 2013 lists Kagulu among Bantu languages with penultimate lengthening. Petzell 2015: 50 states Kagulu has no lexical or grammatical tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in citation forms as transcribed by a CMS missionary (1880s, Mamboya, U-Sagara); accent shifts with suffixation, i.e. computed over the full inflected word. Glottolog/Beidelman 1967 warn the grammar has Gogo material mixed in and many misprints; Marten 2010 calls it 'generally unreliable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Last 1886 describes 'Kagúru' as spoken in U-Sagara around the CMS Mamboya mission (the Kaguru 'sub-tribe' of the Sagara, called Mégi by the Maasai) = Kagulu kagu1239 (autonyms Chikagulu/Chimegi per Petzell 2015). Glottolog's note on this grammar: 'marred with numerous press errors' (Johnston 1922: 791) and 'much Gogo material mixed in it' (Beidelman 1967: 81). Petzell's data (2002-2006) are from Kilosa district (Mamboya/Berega/Gairo), same variety.

new_statements.relation_note: Same passage the catalog's existing statement quotes (Last 1886 p. 3) and the same placement as the catalog penultimate stress (penultimate). Adds the detail that exceptions exist and are marked (mehékulu), that accent shifts with suffixation, and the p. 44 demonstrative final-stress remark. Glottolog notes (after Beidelman 1967) that Last's grammar has 'much Gogo material mixed in it', so the description is of 1880s mission Kagúru and may not be pure Kagulu. Full PDF/EPUB download and page-44 image both returned Google's 'Sorry.. p. 3 was read from the page scan already held by the project.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the penultimate syllable almost without exception; the few words accented elsewhere carry a written acute (mehékulu 'a married woman', i.e. antepenultimate); when suffixes are added the accent moves so that it stays on the new penult, i.e. placement is computed on the whole suffixed word. Separately, in the demonstrative paradigm (p. 44) stress on the final vowel signals greater distance, which is a grammatical (deictic) use of final stress, not the default word pattern.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Almost invariable': lexical exceptions are marked with an acute over the accented syllable, e.g. mehékulu 'a married woman' (antepenult). Accent re-computes to the penult of the suffixed word. On p. 44 (snippet only, page not obtainable) final-vowel stress on demonstratives marks greater distance ('so much the more is the distance denoted'), which is a grammatical exception to penultimate placement.
new_statements.identity_note: Last 1886 describes 'Kagúru' as spoken around the CMS Mamboya mission in the 1880s; Glottolog's reference note (citing Beidelman 1967) warns the grammar has 'much Gogo material mixed in it', so it is not a clean modern Kagulu (G12, kki) description. Petzell's work is on present-day Kagulu of Kilosa/Gairo District, Morogoro Region.

new_statements.quote: Kagulu has alternating stress (or possibly indiscernible lexical stress). In the disyllabic words with penultimate stress there is penultimate vowel lengthening, which is common in Bantu languages. [...] In Kagulu, however, the stress does not seem to be governed by any obvious rules. Each word seems to have a stress pattern of its own. Stress either falls on the penult, on the antepenult, or on the pre-antepenult. Compare the two nouns diˈbiki ‘tree’ and ˈdigoda ‘chair’ [...] In ˈkwinamilahasi ‘to face downwards’, the stress is on the pre-antepenult. The same goes for ˈkutambula ‘to realize’. All this said, stress is quite evenly distributed – even in these multi-syllable words.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog codes Kagulu fixed penultimate from Last 1886: 3 ('accent almost invariable on the penultimate'). Petzell 2008: 41, the modern fieldwork grammar (Berega/Mamboya area speakers), denies a rule: stress 'does not seem to be governed by any obvious rules', falling per word on the penult, antepenult or pre-antepenult, with weak prominence contrasts overall; it concedes penultimate stress with penult lengthening in disyllables. Type differs (lexical/unpredictable and weakly cued vs fixed penult). The statement is hedged ('alternating stress (or possibly indiscernible lexical stress)') and Kraska-Szlenk's 2008 review (held by the project, p. 95) already judged these stress claims 'not v…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Petzell (2008: 40-41) describes Kagulu as non-tonal ('a pitch accent language with limited tonal function'; 'probably phrasal tone and not lexical tone'; no tone marking used) and says word stress is not governed by any obvious rule: each word has its own pattern, with stress on the penult (diˈbiki 'tree'), the antepenult (ˈdigoda 'chair') or the pre-antepenult (ˈkwinamilahasi, ˈkutambula); disyllables with penultimate stress show penultimate vowel lengthening; overall prominence differences are small ('stress is quite evenly distributed.. resembles Japanese.. not completely syllable-timed, however'); prosodic phrasing can regroup syllables across word boundaries (munhu yuya 'that person' phrased munhuyu|ya). p. 40 adds that 'tone and stress show a discrepancy in different Kagulu dialects as well as idiosyncrasies between speakers'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none described (only the hedge 'alternating stress'); no secondary-stress rule given.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenult and pre-antepenult stressed words given as examples (ˈdigoda 'chair', ˈkwinamilahasi 'to face downwards', ˈkutambula 'to realize'); p. 88: the distal demonstrative used emphatically is 'turned into an ideophone. The voice is raised in falsetto towards the end and the last syllable is prolonged: ayuyaaa ‘that (person) far away’' (cf. Last 1886: 44 on final-vowel stress in demonstratives denoting distance); p. 69: 'in Kagulu, constituents are stressed differently. The language does not follow the intonation and stress patterns of, say, English'.
new_statements.identity_note: Petzell describes Kagulu (Chikagulu, G12) as spoken around Berega and Mamboya (Kilosa/Gairo area, Morogoro Region), fieldwork 2002-2005, the 'pure'/mountain (Itumba) variety being the prestige reference; she notes dialects (Tumba, Mangehele; 'Megi' as an exonym) differ 'primarily in intonation'. Last 1886 describes the Kaguru of the CMS Mamboya mission area (Glottolog note: Gogo material mixed). Same language, overlapping area, 120 years apart.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction among texts actually opened: the only primary stress statement is Last 1886 p. 3 (penultimate, with marked lexical exceptions and shift under suffixation), which is what the catalog already records. A potential disagreement is second-hand: Kraska-Szlenk's 2008 review (held by the project, p. 95) says Petzell 2008 pp. 40-41 gives 'not very convincing claims about stress' with examples of 'pre-antepenult' stress that she suggests may be initial stress, and 'probably phrasal tone and not lexical tone'. Petzell 2015 (held by the project, p. 50) and Petzell & Aunio 2019 both state Kagulu has no lexical or grammatical tone, and Hyman 2013's appendix lists G12 Kagulu among penultimate-lengthening languages that lost the PB vowel-length contrast, which is consistent with penultimate prominence. So the modern description (Petzell 2008), which is not open, may complicate the simple penult picture; the catalog's penult reading stands on Last 1886 and is not contradicted by anything opened. Petzell 2008 (= the 2007 dissertation, read here from the author's preprint text, pp. 40-41) contradicts the catalog's fixed-penultimate coding taken from Last 1886: 3. Last: 'the accent is almost invariable on the penultimate', exceptions marked (mehékulu), accent shifting to the new penult under suffixation. Petzell: Kagulu is non-tonal ('pitch accent language with limited tonal function', phrasal not lexical tone) and word stress 'does not seem to be governed by any obvious…
